claims.text: The starting material is as-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a room-temperature yield strength of approximately 1600 MPa.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a yield strength of approximately 855 MPa at about 1000 °C.
A test intervention should replace 10–20% of the Hf content with Al.
Replacing part of Hf with lightweight Al will reduce the density of HfMoTaTiZr.
The Al-modified HfMoTaTiZr alloy will retain a single-phase BCC structure.
Al will dissolve in the BCC lattice of HfMoTaTiZr and induce controlled, moderate lattice distortion.
Al-induced lattice distortion can provide solid-solution strengthening.
A suitable Al substitution level can avoid deleterious intermetallic or brittle secondary phases.
The modified alloy can preserve the high-temperature mechanical robustness of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
The proposed substitution will produce approximately a 10% density decrease.
The modified alloy's room-temperature yield strength will remain within 10% of approximately 1600 MPa.
The modified alloy's yield strength at 1000 °C will remain within 10% of approximately 855 MPa.
The Al-modified alloy will have an improved strength-to-weight ratio relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
Mechanical performance will be evaluated under compressive loading at room temperature and 1000 °C.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires strength to remain within 10% of baseline at both temperatures, but the rejection rule requires a strength loss exceeding 10% at both temperatures. A decisive failure at only one specified temperature would violate the prediction without falsifying it under the stated rule.

The predicted density decrease is approximately 10%, whereas the experiment rejects only decreases below 5%. A result between 5% and 10% would miss the stated prediction but would not trigger rejection.

The boundary requires a single-phase BCC alloy, but the rejection rule addresses only secondary brittle phases that demonstrably compromise ductility or integrity. Any secondary phase violates the boundary even if brittleness is not established.
